databaselibraryreadingslab

“The survival of the past is constantly at the mercy of the present.” §7.2.4 · p. 74

Ray Edmondson, Audiovisual Archiving: Philosophy and Principles, third edition, UNESCO 2016

the work rests on values, and the values have to be examined

  • “All human activity is based on values, assumptions or knowledge of certain truths, even if these are perceived instinctively and not articulated.” §1.1.1 · p. 1
  • “Its starting assumption is that audiovisual archivists need to understand and reflect on their philosophical foundations if they are to exercise their power responsibly.” §1.1.4 · p. 1
  • “why do we do the things we do, and why do we do things the way we do them?” §1.1.5 · p. 1
  • “Audiovisual archivists, like librarians, museologists and other memory professionals, exercise a particular kind of power over the survival, accessibility and interpretation of the world's cultural memory.” §1.1.3 · p. 1

a document is content on a carrier, and neither is the whole of it

The book proposes a definition rather than assuming one, and the definition is a test: a carrier, a content, a device needed to hear or see it, a duration, and a purpose.

§3.3.2.4 · p. 27the book's words
the document“Audiovisual documents are works comprising reproducible images and/or sounds embodied in a carrier”
1 — the device“recording, transmission, perception and comprehension usually requires a technological device”
2 — the duration“visual and/or sonic content has linear duration”
3 — the purpose“purpose is the communication of that content, rather than use of the technology for other purposes”
  • “Moving images and sounds are subjective by nature - they have no objective existence as such.” §5.1.2 · p. 52
  • “one cannot hear a disc by looking at it, nor watch a motion picture by unwinding a film and looking at it” §5.1.2 · p. 52
  • “image and sound recordings, no matter how short, are by their nature linear. They cannot be perceived instantaneously.” §3.3.2.6 · p. 27
  • “Computer games, websites, and other digital creations are, by definition, non-linear in their construction” §3.3.2.8 · p. 28
  • “Content is the sonic, visual or textual information, in either analogue or digital form, resident in the carrier and which is normally migratable to another carrier. The relationship between content and carrier may range from incidental to integral.” §3.2.3.11 · p. 21
  • “In a fundamental sense, content is shaped by carrier and context.” §5.3.14 · p. 58
  • “Pop songs still last for about 3 minutes because this was the playing time of an Edison cylinder or 78 rpm disc.” §5.3.14 · p. 58

preservation and access are two sides of one coin

  • “Preservation and access are two sides of the same coin.” §3.2.6.1 · p. 23
  • “Preservation is necessary to ensure permanent accessibility; yet preservation is not an end in itself. Without the objective of access it has no point.” §3.2.6.2 · p. 23
  • “Preservation is the totality of things necessary to ensure the permanent accessibility - forever - of an audiovisual document with the maximum integrity.” §3.2.6.3 · p. 24
  • “Nothing has ever been preserved - at best, it is being preserved!” §3.2.6.5 · p. 24
  • “Audiovisual documents, like other documents, have two components: the audio and/or visual content and the carrier on which they reside.” §5.3.3 · p. 56
  • “the retention of original carriers for their viable life spans - regardless of what copies have been made - becomes a fundamental matter of curatorial integrity” §7.3.1.3 · p. 75
  • “Some carriers, such as shellac and vinyl pressings and some film stocks, may have a potential shelf life of hundreds of years. The life expectancy of CDs, DVDs and magnetic audio and videotape is far less certain” §5.1.5 · p. 53
  • “Content migration is never an entirely benign process, because it involves trade-offs and on-balance decisions about the quality and character of the result.” §5.1.6 · p. 53

digitization answers a different question than preservation

  • “When digitizing analogue materials, the option to go back to the original format to repeat the process remains. For digitally-born works, there is no such option. If they are missed, they may be quickly lost.” §1.4.2 · p. 4
  • “The preservation of motion picture film recognises that it has both analogue and digital aspects: the image, comprising randomly distributed crystals in gelatin, is analogue, but the sampling of the photographic subject at the rate of 24 frames per second is digital in concept and execution.” §5.1.6 · p. 53
  • “Nor is operational but obsolete technology much use without the skills to run and maintain it. Once they are no longer part of the industry mainstream, such skills become esoteric: the province of the individual enthusiast and the audiovisual archive.” §5.3.12 · p. 58
  • “It may therefore be that the greatest challenge of digitization is not one of technology or economics, but of scholarship, education and ethics.” §5.4.11 · p. 61
  • “in the case of an audiovisual work, it's often just the title. How does a reader know what copy the writer accessed? Was it analog or digital? Was it complete? What was the provenance? Where was the copy held?” §5.4.12 · p. 61
  • “The unmediated use and misuse of archival material - for example, the broadcasting or sale of poor quality copies, or the cliché of running of old footage at the wrong speed in television documentaries - devalues it and creates erroneous perceptions of its character and significance.” §3.2.6.8 · p. 25

a reconstruction is a new version, not a restoration

  • “A reconstruction is a new version of a work accomplished by bringing together incomplete or fragmentary elements from multiple sources and rearranging them into a coherent whole, sometimes with considerable manipulation of images and/or sound and the use of bridging devices, for a defined access purpose and usually for public presentation.” appendix 3 · p. 86
  • “A reconstruction differs from a restoration, which involves the removal of the accretions of age - such as surface noise, visual artefacts, scratches and damage - from a preservation copy, but does not involve manipulation of its content in any way.” appendix 3 · p. 86

the archivist decides what the future knows

  • “The nature of the digital media opens up entirely new possibilities for manipulating sounds and images to falsify history, without leaving any trace of such action.” §7.3.1.4 · p. 75
  • “Blind obedience and going with the flow is always the easiest course but, as history shows, it is often the wrong one.” §7.4.4.4 · p. 79
  • “They make life or death choices about what shall be saved or discarded. They decide timing and the form in which it will survive.” §7.6.2 · p. 81
  • “the choice of what is promoted or suppressed, and how it is presented” §7.6.3 · p. 81
  • “Collective memory has moved from a manual to a technological concept.” §8.1 · p. 82
  • “The number of people engaged in the task worldwide barely reaches five figures, and even that is probably an overestimate. This small community, committed and tenacious, yet largely unknown and unsung, carries an immense responsibility.” §8.3 · p. 82
  • “How they use it now will determine much of what posterity knows of this age.” §8.3 · p. 82
  • “The philosophy and principles of audiovisual archiving will always be a work in progress.” §8.2 · p. 82

source: writings/Audiovisual Archiving.pdf — Ray Edmondson, Audiovisual Archiving: Philosophy and Principles, third edition (UNESCO, 2016), 102 pages. Paragraph numbers and page numbers are the book's own; appendix 2's table is redrawn from the book.
